document.title: FDG PET distribution atlas of neurodegenerative disease
document.subtitle: Region-level hypo- and hypermetabolism patterns for 35 entities, coded on the Desikan-Killiany parcellation for 3-D rendering
document.purpose: Machine-readable source for a 3-D brain atlas. Every pattern is an ordinal, region-level statement drawn from the published literature; no continuous SUVR or z-score scale is implied, because none exists across this differential.
document.honestHeadline: FDG PET is a sensitive, non-specific test. Only a handful of the patterns here have published accuracy figures, most of those come from enriched two-way comparisons, and several widely taught signs have none at all. Read `publishedAccuracy` and `evidenceNote` before using any pattern as a rule-in.
document.revisionNote: v1.1: publishedAccuracy/discriminator text reconciled with the audited flowchart JSON (AD specificity range, IMT provenance, epilepsy statistic, Minoshima 2001 verified). Region codes unchanged.

parcellation.name: Desikan-Killiany cortical parcellation with FreeSurfer aseg subcortical segmentation
parcellation.labelConvention: FreeSurfer LUT (1000-1035 left cortex, 2000-2035 right cortex, aseg values for deep structures)
knownLimits: Anterior and posterior portions of the superior, middle and inferior temporal gyri cannot be separated; 'anterior temporal' is carried by temporal pole and entorhinal cortex.
There is no mammillary body, periaqueductal grey, tectal plate, hypothalamus, substantia nigra, subthalamic nucleus, dentate nucleus, cerebellar vermis or middle cerebellar peduncle parcel.
The insula is not visible on an unopened lateral surface, so it is carried as a deep structure in the 3-D views.
The brainstem sub-division is derived by MNI z-coordinate and is an approximation, not a FreeSurfer label.

encoding.note: Severity is ordinal. `evidenceClass` distinguishes a published sparing claim from an assumption — never render them identically.
encoding.unassignedMeaning: A region absent from a pattern is NOT a claim that it is normal — it means no source states its state.

entities.name: Typical amnestic AD
entities.summary: Posterior cingulate and precuneus first, then bilateral temporoparietal association cortex, with primary cortices, deep grey, brainstem and cerebellum preserved.
entities.discriminator: Posterior midline + temporoparietal loss with an intact sensorimotor strip and intact primary visual cortex.
entities.mainMimic: DLB (adds occipital, spares posterior cingulate); depression can reproduce the pattern completely and reversibly.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Sensitivity 84–94%, specificity 63–74% against autopsy — a sensitive, not a specific, test. The three source series overlap in patients, so this is not three independent confirmations.

patterns.label: Classic amnestic AD
patterns.evidenceNote: Replicated across autopsy-validated series; the best-characterised pattern in the field.
patterns.asymmetry: Commonly mildly asymmetric; side not disease-determined.
patterns.caveat: The hippocampus is deliberately left unshaded. It is NOT a sparing claim — hippocampal FDG is simply not reliably measurable (low baseline metabolism, partial-volume effect), so use MRI volumetry for the medial temporal lobe. Frontal association cortex is left unshaded here and appears in the advanced pattern.

entities.name: Posterior cortical atrophy
entities.summary: Occipitoparietal and occipitotemporal hypometabolism, markedly asymmetric, often right-predominant, with frontal and anterior temporal sparing.
entities.discriminator: Marked asymmetry of parietal/occipital loss — PCA 94% vs DLB 31% (sens 94%, spec 69%); asymmetric cingulate island sign PCA 63% vs DLB 9%.
entities.mainMimic: DLB is the great mimic — the cingulate island sign is present in 50% of PCA and the quantitative ratio does not differ (p=0.43). Heidenhain CJD; eyes-closed acquisition, which fabricates occipital hypometabolism.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Asymmetry sens 94% / spec 69%; asymmetric CIS spec 92% / sens 31%.

patterns.label: Classic PCA
patterns.evidenceNote: Crutch 2017 consensus requires predominant occipitoparietal or occipitotemporal hypometabolism, hypoperfusion or atrophy.
patterns.asymmetry: Asymmetry itself is the sign. Drawn right-predominant because that is the commoner side — 10 of 15 asymmetric cases — but roughly one in three is LEFT-predominant, so a left-sided plate is equally diagnostic.
patterns.caveat: Temporal pole, orbitofrontal and caudate involvement points away from PCA and toward DLB — but these are frequency differences (temporal pole sens 92% / spec 72%; caudate 85% / 71%), not absolutes: PCA does involve the striatum and thalamus, which is why they are shaded mild here rather than marked spared. The 63%-versus-9% asymmetric-CIS figure has as its denominator the cases that had a cingulate island at all (8 of 16 PCA), which is why the sensitivity against all PCA is only 31%.

entities.name: Logopenic variant PPA
entities.summary: Left temporoparietal junction — posterior superior and middle temporal gyri, angular gyrus, inferior parietal lobule, often extending to precuneus and posterior cingulate.
entities.discriminator: Left temporoparietal junction focus with spared anterior temporal poles and spared frontal operculum.
entities.mainMimic: nfvPPA at onset; amyloid-negative lvPPA is a distinct FTLD-TDP subtype.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Across a mixed PPA + AD + CBS cohort, FDG predicted amyloid status with 84% accuracy versus 65–67% for clinical assessment alone (Taswell 2015 — the cohort was not lvPPA alone). Amyloid PET positive in 96% (25/26); autopsy AD 11/11.

patterns.label: Right-predominant lvPPA
patterns.evidenceNote: About 26% of series by visual reading (lower with quantitative asymmetry cut-offs), despite the criteria specifying left.
patterns.caveat: Right-predominant cases extend into the non-dominant frontal lobe, so the frontal operculum is NOT drawn as spared here even though it is in the classic left-predominant pattern.

patterns.label: Amyloid-negative lvPPA (FTLD-TDP)
patterns.evidenceNote: A distinct subtype: extensive LEFT-hemisphere involvement reaching the anterior temporal pole, hippocampus, caudate and fusiform — regions the amyloid-positive form spares.
patterns.asymmetry: Left, and more extensive anteriorly than amyloid-positive lvPPA.
patterns.caveat: The published figures for this subtype — right lateral temporal sens 67% / spec 100%, asymmetric hippocampal metabolism sens 83% — could not be traced to a primary source and should not be quoted.

entities.name: Behavioural / dysexecutive AD
entities.typicalAge: Often <65 y (mean 54 y in the dysexecutive series)
entities.summary: Usually an AD-like posterior pattern in which frontal involvement is MILDER than in bvFTD — not absent. The intuitive 'frontal AD' is the minority phenotype.
entities.discriminator: A bvFTD-like syndrome with a posterior-predominant FDG pattern; frontal and insular involvement is present but milder than bvFTD, and the posterior deficit is the more conspicuous one.
entities.mainMimic: bvFTD — and FDG has poor discriminative power for this pair, so Core 1 biomarkers are mandatory.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Amyloid PET positive 22/22 and tau PET positive 20/20 in the dysexecutive series; no FDG accuracy figure exists for bvAD versus bvFTD.

patterns.label: Behavioural AD — posterior pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: The majority phenotype in the published behavioural-AD series.
patterns.caveat: Routinely mislabelled bvFTD, and the reverse error is also common. The correct statement is LESS frontal involvement than bvFTD, not frontal sparing — bvAD shows bilateral insular and right lateral frontal involvement. Medial temporal structures are left unshaded because nothing establishes their state in the behavioural phenotype.

entities.name: Autosomal-dominant AD (PSEN1, PSEN2, APP)
entities.summary: Core AD temporoparietal and posterior midline pattern, with a more posterior, parieto-occipital predominance than late-onset AD.
entities.discriminator: Young onset plus a posterior/parieto-occipital predominance plus a dominant family history. NOT striatal FDG: striatum-FIRST deposition in this disease is an AMYLOID finding, and the DIAN regional analysis specifically found no corresponding caudate FDG abnormality.
entities.mainMimic: If striatal hypometabolism is present it can prompt a wrong turn toward Huntington disease, CBD or DLB — anchor on the coexisting precuneus signature and the family history.
entities.publishedAccuracy: No FDG accuracy figures; the DIAN cascade puts parietal and precuneus hypometabolism about 10 years before expected onset.

patterns.label: Symptomatic ADAD
patterns.evidenceNote: DIAN and related cohorts; striatal amyloid deposition is the anatomical correlate of the striatal FDG finding.
patterns.caveat: Only 5–10% of early-onset AD is autosomal dominant; most young-onset AD is sporadic. The caudate is shaded only mild, and the putamen and thalamus not at all: the striatal signature of this disease is amyloid deposition, and the presymptomatic thalamus/caudate finding usually quoted is an MRI volumetric result, not an FDG one.

patterns.label: Presymptomatic carrier
patterns.evidenceNote: DIAN: FDG precuneus hypometabolism about 10 years before expected onset; thalamic change reported in presymptomatic PSEN1 carriers.
patterns.caveat: Presymptomatic imaging is research practice, not clinical care. Lateral parietal metabolism is already falling in this window, so it is drawn mild rather than spared. A HYPERmetabolic phase in precuneus and posterior cingulate is described earlier still, before the decline — an early carrier scan can therefore look hot, not cold, in exactly the signature region.

entities.name: Down syndrome–associated AD
entities.summary: Classic AD topography — posterior cingulate and precuneus first, then temporoparietal, then frontal, with occipital and sensorimotor sparing.
entities.discriminator: The topography is ordinary AD; the diagnostic problem is the baseline, not the pattern.
entities.mainMimic: Hypothyroidism, obstructive sleep apnoea (~50%), depression, coeliac disease, atlantoaxial myelopathy, sensory loss and medication effects — all common and reversible.
entities.publishedAccuracy: No FDG accuracy figures in this population.

patterns.label: AD in Down syndrome
patterns.evidenceNote: Ordered ADAD-like cascade documented across the 3rd–6th decades.
patterns.caveat: Sparing is drawn as INFERRED throughout: the topography is assumed to follow sporadic AD and no Down-syndrome-specific FDG topography study underlies it. Standard AD z-score databases WILL over-call, because younger adults with Down syndrome and no dementia show frank HYPERmetabolism in prefrontal, sensorimotor, thalamic and inferior temporal/entorhinal cortex — the very regions drawn as spared. Age- and DS-matched normative data are mandatory.

entities.name: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy and CAA-related inflammation
entities.summary: No established diagnostic FDG pattern. Regional hypometabolism follows the haemorrhagic and ischaemic burden; in CAA-ri it follows the confluent white-matter oedema.
entities.discriminator: There is none on FDG. The diagnosis is made on SWI/GRE and the Boston criteria v2.0.
entities.mainMimic: An AD posterior pattern appears when AD co-pathology is present, which is common.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Boston v2.0 versus autopsy: sens 74.5%, spec 95.0%, AUC 0.848 (autopsy subset, n=150) — for the MRI criteria, not for FDG. In non-haemorrhagic presentations, which is who reaches a cognitive clinic, sensitivity falls to 55.1%.

patterns.label: Lobar burden–following pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: ILLUSTRATIVE, not a signature. Drawn at a single uniform grade to make the point that the deficit follows lesions rather than a syndrome.
patterns.asymmetry: Follows the lesions; frequently strikingly asymmetric. Nothing about the symmetric map drawn here should be read as characteristic.
patterns.caveat: There is no CAA FDG signature; this map is a lesion-burden illustration only. Deep grey, cerebellum and brainstem are drawn as inferred sparing because the Boston criteria require STRICTLY LOBAR haemorrhage — that is a haemorrhage topography argument, not a metabolic finding. Amyloid PET is positive in CAA because it binds vascular Aβ, and cannot separate CAA from parenchymal AD.

patterns.label: Classic DLB
patterns.evidenceNote: Autopsy-validated for the occipital sign; the cingulate island sign is a rule-in sign with poor negative predictive value.
patterns.caveat: The cingulate island is RELATIVE preservation, not normal metabolism — it is defined as the ratio of posterior cingulate to precuneus PLUS cuneus, which is why the precuneus must be shaded for the sign to exist at all. The island is abolished by AD co-pathology: the ratio falls as Braak stage rises (r=−0.96, p<0.001), and the sign is absent in both prodromal and advanced disease. The striatum is NOT spared in DLB — caudate hypometabolism has 85% sensitivity for DLB over PCA, which is exactly why it is a PCA discriminator.

patterns.label: AD-like phenotype (~29% of DLB)
patterns.evidenceNote: Mosconi 2008 — about 29% of DLB shows an AD-like cortical pattern.
patterns.caveat: About 29% of DLB looks like this. The island is gone and FDG cannot make the call — use DaT SPECT or cardiac MIBG.

patterns.label: PDD — as for DLB
patterns.evidenceNote: Meles 2017: no individual-level metabolic separation from DLB.
patterns.caveat: The cortical map here is deliberately IDENTICAL to the DLB plate, because the two are not separable on FDG. What is added is the PD-related covariance pattern: relative hypermetabolism of putamen, pallidum, thalamus, sensorimotor cortex, pons and cerebellum. That is a covariance-network weight, not measured hypermetabolism, and it is the mirror image of the MSA pattern. Do not build an FDG-based DLB-versus-PDD branch.

entities.name: Behavioural variant FTD
entities.summary: Frontomedial and dorsal anterior cingulate, orbitofrontal, dorsolateral prefrontal, anterior insula and anterior temporal poles, with caudate involvement and an anterior–posterior gradient that is the mirror image of AD.
entities.discriminator: Preserved posterior cingulate, precuneus and lateral temporoparietal cortex — the most useful negative region on the scan.
entities.mainMimic: Primary psychiatric disorder (specificity 68–93%); the phenocopy syndrome (M:F ≈10:1, normal imaging, non-progressive over ≥3 y); behavioural AD.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Frontal and/or anterior-temporal pattern on 3D-SSP: spec 97.6%, sens 86%, LR+ 36.5, κ 0.78 (n=45, fully autopsy-confirmed) — but that was a forced binary AD-versus-FTD choice in a cohort enriched 31:14. Against an open differential the numbers fall hard: FDG alone in late-onset behavioural change sens 90% / spec 68% (n=111), rising to 93% against dedicated psychiatric comparators.

patterns.evidenceNote: Devenney/D'Souza: normal MRI and normal FDG, non-progressive over ≥3 y.

entities.name: Semantic variant PPA
entities.summary: Bilateral anterior temporal poles, left predominant, extending to orbitofrontal cortex, fusiform gyrus, insula and anterior cingulate.
entities.discriminator: Anterior temporal focus with preserved posterior temporoparietal cortex and preserved precuneus — the opposite of lvPPA.
entities.mainMimic: Arachnoid cysts and other structural lesions produce anterior temporal hypometabolism mimicking svPPA — always read with the co-registered MRI or CT.
entities.publishedAccuracy: SPM-based classification of svPPA: sens 100% / spec 93.1% / accuracy 94%; AUC 0.98 versus AD and 0.91 versus bvFTD. No AUTOPSY-confirmed accuracy study exists — every series is clinically defined and n<50. FTLD-TDP type C in 83% at autopsy.

entities.name: Genetic FTD — C9orf72 / GRN / MAPT
entities.summary: Three genotype-linked variations on the FTD pattern: C9orf72 adds bilateral thalamic hypometabolism, GRN is markedly asymmetric with parietal extension, MAPT is symmetric and anteromedial temporal.
entities.discriminator: Bilateral thalamic hypometabolism for C9orf72 — AUC 0.909 for C9+ versus C9− FTLD, with a reduced thalamus/pons ratio (p<0.01).
entities.mainMimic: Each genotype pattern overlaps sporadic bvFTD; C9orf72 may present psychiatrically or as a Huntington phenocopy.
entities.publishedAccuracy: C9orf72 thalamic AUC 0.909 — this one IS an FDG result (n=22 C9+, 22 C9−, 23 controls). The GENFI asymmetry indices (GRN 4.41 > C9orf72 2.92 > MAPT 2.20) and the GRN and MAPT topographies come from MRI VOLUMETRY, not FDG; no equivalent FDG series exists. GENFI tested GRN vs MAPT (p<0.001) and GRN vs C9orf72 (p=0.009) but not C9orf72 vs MAPT.

entities.name: Progressive supranuclear palsy
entities.summary: Midbrain and upper brainstem hypometabolism — the signature finding — with medial frontal, anterior cingulate and SMA/premotor involvement, caudate more than putamen, and medial thalamus. Symmetric.
entities.discriminator: Symmetry is the key discriminator from CBS. Midbrain involvement is the discriminator from iNPH, which spares it.
entities.mainMimic: iNPH (magnetic gait, falls, frontal slowing, urinary urgency — but the midbrain is preserved); anti-IgLON5 disease, which gives a PSP-like syndrome with DIFFUSE rather than midbrain-focal hypometabolism.
entities.publishedAccuracy: PSPRP automated pattern sens 88% / spec 94% / PPV 91% (secondary-sourced). Independent prospective validation: whole cohort sens 100% / spec 94%; with symptom duration ≤2 y sens 100% / spec 100% (n=77). Against idiopathic PD the range is far wider — sens 52.9–75%, spec 80–100%, AUC 0.80. Real-world routine performance is lower still: pooled CBD+PSP sens 0.62, spec 0.97.

patterns.label: Classic PSP-Richardson
patterns.evidenceNote: Frontal hypometabolism in 97% overall — 100% in PSP-SL, PSP-CBS and PSP-F, 73% in PSP-PGF.
patterns.asymmetry: Symmetric — this is the key discriminator from CBS.
patterns.caveat: No isolated-sign specificity has ever been published for midbrain hypometabolism — every published figure is for the composite pattern. The pons is deliberately drawn only mild: it is the DENOMINATOR of the midbrain/pons ratio and of the MR parkinsonism index, and shading it as heavily as the midbrain would erase the contrast the sign depends on. The cerebellum is marked inferred rather than published, because it is conventionally the intensity-normalisation reference in PSP series. Frontal hypometabolism was present in 97% overall, but the phenotype cells are small — PSP-CBS n=6.

patterns.label: PSP-CBS phenotype
patterns.evidenceNote: Pardini: markedly asymmetric anterior medial frontal / anterior cingulate.
patterns.asymmetry: Markedly asymmetric — the side is patient-determined and contralateral to the affected limb. The left-sided plate is an ARBITRARY example; mirror it for a left-limb presentation.
patterns.caveat: In PSP-CBS, exclude AD by CSF or amyloid PET — a mandatory context-dependent exclusion in the MDS criteria. The midbrain shading here is extrapolated from PSP-Richardson: the autopsy-defined CBS-PSP subgroup (n=5) showed NO midbrain cluster.

entities.name: Corticobasal syndrome
entities.summary: Markedly asymmetric frontoparietal and perirolandic hypometabolism with basal ganglia and thalamic involvement, contralateral to the affected limb, and crossed cerebellar diaschisis.
entities.discriminator: The precentral gyrus is the only region hypometabolic across all pathological substrates — the anatomical anchor of CBS. Asymmetry separates it from PSP.
entities.mainMimic: CBS is a syndrome, not a pathology: CBD 33.3%, PSP 29.2%, AD 12.5%, FTLD-TDP 6.3%, GGT 4.2%, DLB 4.2% at autopsy.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Sens 75–91% with specificity usually above 90% in the pattern-analysis literature; real-world pooled 4R-tauopathy sens 0.62 / spec 0.97. Sensitivity is the problem, not specificity — a normal-looking scan does not exclude CBS. For detecting AD as the substrate of CBS: pooled NPV 97%, LR− 0.06, PPV 68%, LR+ 3.90 — a good rule-out and a poor rule-in.

patterns.evidenceNote: Pardini's pathology-specific patterns rest on n=14/10/5 with no accuracy metrics — directional heuristics only.
patterns.asymmetry: Markedly asymmetric, contralateral to the affected limb — the side is patient-determined. The left-sided plate is an ARBITRARY example; mirror it for a left-limb presentation.
patterns.caveat: Sensorimotor sparing — the hallmark of AD — is LOST in CBS-CBD. Crossed cerebellar diaschisis is commonest in CBS of any diagnosis, and it invalidates cerebellar intensity normalisation.

patterns.label: CBS-AD — asymmetric posterior, no deep grey
patterns.evidenceNote: Pardini n=10; amyloid positivity in CBS is 44% by PET but only ~12–25% at autopsy, because of age-related incidental amyloid.
patterns.asymmetry: Asymmetric — the side is patient-determined. The left-sided plate is an ARBITRARY example.
patterns.caveat: The deep grey sparing here IS a published negative — no cluster of hypometabolism was found in the thalami or basal ganglia in the autopsy-defined CBS-AD subgroup. But the precentral gyrus is NOT spared: it is the one region hypometabolic across every pathological substrate of CBS, which is why it is drawn mild rather than preserved. Amyloid PET or CSF/plasma AD biomarkers are mandatory in every CBS.

entities.name: Multiple system atrophy
entities.summary: MSA-P: posterior and dorsolateral putaminal hypometabolism, often asymmetric early, plus pons and cerebellum even in the parkinsonian phenotype. MSA-C: pons, middle cerebellar peduncles and cerebellar hemispheres, usually with putaminal involvement.
entities.discriminator: Putamen plus pons plus cerebellum together. This is the inverse of PD, which shows relative hypermetabolism of putamen/pallidum, thalamus, sensorimotor cortex, pons and cerebellum.
entities.mainMimic: Genetic spinocerebellar ataxias — the hot cross bun sign is not specific and occurs in SCA1/2/3/6/7/8, FXTAS, vCJD, Wilson disease, autoimmune cerebellitis, CTX and pontine infarct.
entities.publishedAccuracy: MSARP automated sens 85% / spec 96% / PPV 97% (secondary-sourced); meta-analytic range 77–96% sens, >90% spec; real-world routine sens 1.00 / spec 0.91. But independent prospective validation is much weaker and MSA is the pattern that degrades most early: sens 79% whole cohort, 73% at ≤2 y symptom duration.

entities.name: Anti-IgLON5 disease
entities.summary: DIFFUSE cortical hypometabolism, as opposed to the regionally restricted midbrain / medial-frontal / striatal pattern of PSP.
entities.discriminator: A PSP-like syndrome with diffuse rather than midbrain-focal hypometabolism should trigger an IgLON5 antibody test.
entities.mainMimic: PSP, MSA, fatal familial insomnia, Morvan/CASPR2 syndrome, narcolepsy, Huntington disease in the chorea phenotype.
entities.publishedAccuracy: No FDG accuracy figures, and the evidence base is very thin: the FDG claim rests on roughly 5–10 scanned patients described only as showing widespread cortical hypometabolism, with no published regional breakdown. The parcel-level grading here is therefore ILLUSTRATIVE of a diffuse pattern, not measured. Serum IgLON5 IgG positive in 98%, CSF in 88%.

patterns.label: Diffuse cortical pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: Jia 2026 — the contrast with PSP's focal pattern is the diagnostic point.
patterns.caveat: The subcortical structures are deliberately NOT shaded as hypometabolic. The midbrain, pons, caudate, putamen and thalamus finding usually attached to this disease is TAU-PET binding, not FDG hypometabolism — and shading the midbrain would destroy the only discriminator that matters here, which is diffuse cortical loss versus PSP's midbrain-focal loss. This entity is partially treatable: 41% improved with short-term immunotherapy and 75% showed no further progression on long-term therapy. Antibody titres do not track disease activity, and a poor response does not refute the diagnosis.

entities.name: Huntington disease and HD phenocopies
entities.summary: Bilateral caudate more than putamen hypometabolism, present in manifest and premanifest carriers, with relative cerebellar and pontine hypermetabolism.
entities.discriminator: Caudate-dominant striatal loss with an otherwise preserved cortex early. Cortical involvement appears later and tracks cognitive decline.
entities.mainMimic: C9orf72 phenocopies show a frontotemporal/insular ± caudate pattern, not a pure HD pattern. Overall genetic yield in HD phenocopies is only ~2.4%.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Caudate FDG below a cut-off of 1.0493 separated converters from non-converters over ≥5 y (p<0.0001), independent of CAG size, improving age-at-onset prediction by 37%. EANM-EAN graded the evidence 'poor' and did not endorse clinical use in presymptomatic HD.

patterns.label: Manifest HD
patterns.evidenceNote: Consistent across manifest and premanifest cohorts.
patterns.caveat: The 'hot posterior fossa' is a normalisation effect against a dead striatum, not true hypermetabolism. Caudate atrophy causes partial-volume loss that inflates apparent hypometabolism — effect sizes shrink after correction.

patterns.label: Premanifest carrier
patterns.evidenceNote: Caudate hypometabolism precedes motor onset and predicts conversion.
patterns.caveat: Cortical sparing here is a PUBLISHED negative: premanifest carriers did not show cortical hypometabolism in the direct comparison against early-symptomatic patients, who did. Representative parcels are marked rather than every lobe, because the source made a regional statement, not a parcel-level measurement. Striatal hypometabolism in premanifest carriers is significant on quantitative analysis, not on visual reading. HTT CAG repeat sizing is the confirmatory test; FDG is never confirmatory.

entities.name: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis without dementia
entities.summary: Hypometabolism in primary motor/precentral and premotor cortex, frontal cortex and inferolateral parietal cortex, with relative hypermetabolism of the midbrain and upper brainstem, medial temporal cortex, cerebellum and occipital pole.
entities.discriminator: Motor-strip hypometabolism together with relative HYPERmetabolism of the brainstem, cerebellum, medial temporal cortex and occipital pole — the hypermetabolic signature is the more defensible half of the pattern.
entities.mainMimic: Hypermetabolic midbrain and medial-temporal clusters can be misread as encephalitis or tumour.

patterns.label: ALS
patterns.evidenceNote: EANM-EAN graded the ALS evidence 'good' but still did not endorse clinical use.
patterns.asymmetry: Usually symmetric; may follow the clinically affected side.
patterns.caveat: The hypermetabolism is relative and normalisation-dependent — but unlike the 'hot posterior fossa' of Huntington disease it may have a biological substrate (neuroinflammation with activated microglia), and medullary uptake tracks survival. Hypermetabolic midbrain and medial-temporal clusters are routinely MISREAD as encephalitis or tumour. The posterior cingulate is drawn mild, not spared: it is named among the most discriminating regions in the source series. Extensive frontotemporal hypometabolism predicts much shorter survival — 20.1 versus 51.3 months. The accuracy figures came from a comparison with 20 screened healthy controls, and 10 primary lateral sclerosis patients showed a similar pattern in the same study.

entities.name: LATE / LANS — limbic-predominant amnestic neurodegenerative syndrome
entities.summary: Medial temporal (amygdala and hippocampus) with anterior/temporopolar, orbitofrontal and superior medial frontal hypometabolism — the mirror image of the AD signature.
entities.discriminator: Precuneus, posterior cingulate and lateral temporoparietal cortex PRESERVED — the single most useful negative finding. The inferior-to-medial-temporal ratio is HIGH (Botha 2018; Buciuc 2020) (autopsy LATE-NC versus AD); in AD it is low.
entities.mainMimic: FDG cannot separate LATE from PART or argyrophilic grain disease — all three converge on the same limbic phenotype. Burnt-out autoimmune limbic encephalitis and temporal lobe epilepsy give the same picture.
entities.publishedAccuracy: IMT ratio proposed by Botha 2018 and tested against autopsy TDP-43 status by Buciuc 2020 (73 cases; IMT + frontal supraorbital metabolism identified up to 81% of TDP-43-positive cases); the autopsy-derived LATE-NC signature (Grothe 2023) rests on 7 LATE-NC vs 23 AD cases. No validated single-ratio AUC. LANS balanced accuracy 74.6% (Mayo) / 73.3% (ADNI).

patterns.label: Limbic-predominant pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: Applied to ADNI, 10% of clinically diagnosed AD had a LATE-like FDG pattern; those patients were 10 years older and declined more slowly.
patterns.caveat: The INFERIOR TEMPORAL gyrus is deliberately drawn as preserved: it is the denominator of the inferior-to-medial-temporal ratio, and it is RELATIVELY preserved in LATE compared with AD (d=−0.91). Shade it and the discriminator disappears. Pure LATE is rare (~2–3% of dementia even in the oldest old); mixed ADNC + LATE-NC dominates, so a binary AD-versus-LATE branch misrepresents the biology. Limbic hypometabolism is uncommon even in confirmed cases — present in 3 of 4 autopsy LATE-NC, 15 of 33 mixed and 9 of 53 pure AD. Partial-volume effect is worst in exactly the region being measured.

entities.name: Hippocampal sclerosis of ageing versus mesial temporal sclerosis
entities.summary: Hippocampal sclerosis of ageing gives limbic hypometabolism confined to the medial temporal and orbitofrontal territory. Mesial temporal sclerosis gives broad ipsilateral temporal hypometabolism extending well beyond the hippocampus.
entities.discriminator: The WIDTH of the temporal deficit is the discriminator: epilepsy spreads laterally to the lateral temporal cortex, temporal pole, ipsilateral thalamus and frontal operculum; LATE/HS-A stays limbic and orbitofrontal.
entities.mainMimic: Burnt-out autoimmune limbic encephalitis produces the same picture.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Simultaneous FDG PET/MRI in a surgical cohort (n=98) gave sens 95.3% / spec 8.8% for predicting post-operative seizure freedom — a surgical-outcome statistic for the combined modality, not a differential-diagnosis one.

patterns.label: Mesial temporal sclerosis / TLE
patterns.evidenceNote: The lateral spread is the classic interictal finding and is characteristically larger than the epileptogenic zone.

patterns.caveat: In an older adult with an amnestic syndrome and medial temporal FDG change, ask about discrete episodes and morning attacks and get an EEG before committing to LATE or LANS.

entities.name: Vascular cognitive impairment (subcortical ischaemic type)
entities.summary: Scattered, patchy focal cortical AND subcortical defects concordant with MRI lesions, extending diffusely to both hemispheres, basal ganglia, thalamus and cerebellum — more widespread and less region-selective than AD.
entities.discriminator: The AD-specific sparing profile — primary cortices, basal ganglia, cerebellum — is NOT preserved. The ratio of association-area to primary+deep+cerebellar metabolism is significantly lower in AD than in vascular disease.
entities.mainMimic: AD, and the two coexist far more often than either occurs alone.
entities.publishedAccuracy: EANM-EAN graded the evidence for AD versus vascular dementia as 'lacking' — clinical use rests on panel opinion only.

patterns.label: Subcortical ischaemic VCI
patterns.evidenceNote: Descriptive; the pattern follows the lesions, which is the point.
patterns.asymmetry: Asymmetric and patchy by nature. The left-predominant plate is an ARBITRARY example — the distribution follows this patient's lesions.
patterns.caveat: No 'mixed AD + vascular' plate is drawn, deliberately: mixed disease means both biomarker sets are positive, not that the FDG looks halfway between two pictures. Note the crossed cerebellar diaschisis — the cerebellum opposite the dominant hemispheric burden. Cortical deafferentation from subcortical lesions produces cortical hypometabolism with no cortical lesion, so FDG 'sees' more than MRI. In vascular disease every conventional intensity-normalisation region may be compromised. Do not attempt to attribute proportions between AD and vascular contributions.

entities.name: Technical and pharmacological artefact — the validity gate
entities.summary: Eyes closed during uptake fabricates occipital hypometabolism and with it a DLB or Heidenhain pattern. Sedation gives a global reduction with disproportionate thalamic and occipital decrement. Hyperglycaemia progressively reduces uptake.
entities.discriminator: None — this is a pre-read gate, not a diagnosis. The artefact is excluded by the acquisition record, not by the images.
entities.mainMimic: It mimics whatever the reader is looking for. PET/CT misregistration gives reduced activity on the attenuation-corrected images with a normal non-corrected image.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Not applicable. The reference region can change WHICH DISEASE the z-map suggests. Three further gate failures cannot be drawn on a parcellation at all and must be checked from the acquisition record: hyperglycaemia (uptake falls progressively above ~110 mg/dL; >160–180 mg/dL is the outer limit and insulin rescue does not work — reschedule), PET/CT misregistration, and normal-database mismatch.

patterns.label: Eyes-closed acquisition
patterns.evidenceNote: Specified in the SNMMI procedure standard (eyes open, dimly lit room).
patterns.caveat: Everything except the occipital cortex is drawn as preserved, because that is the whole point: a normal brain scanned with the eyes shut. Note how closely this counterfeits DLB — occipital loss with an intact posterior cingulate. It is the single commonest way to manufacture a DLB pattern. Record the eye state during uptake.

patterns.label: Benzodiazepine / sedation effect
patterns.evidenceNote: Global reduction with disproportionate thalamic and occipital decrement.
patterns.caveat: The reduction is GLOBAL — every cortical parcel is shaded — and that is exactly why it is dangerous: intensity normalisation cancels the global component, so what survives on a z-map is only the relative thalamic and occipital decrement, which looks like a focal finding. Guidance requires FDG to be given at least 15 minutes before any sedation.

entities.name: Primary psychiatric disorder / depressive pseudodementia
entities.summary: Often normal; or frontal and dorsal anterior cingulate hypometabolism with the posterior cingulate and precuneus characteristically spared.
entities.discriminator: A normal scan largely excludes neurodegeneration. FDG is a good rule-OUT and a mediocre rule-IN for bvFTD.
entities.mainMimic: bvFTD — reported specificity against psychiatric disorder spans 68–93%, and 40% of false-positive scans had a primary psychiatric diagnosis.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Reported specificity of FDG against primary psychiatric disorder spans 68–93% — at the upper bound, sens 87% / spec 93% / accuracy 88% against dedicated psychiatric comparators. EANM-EAN graded the evidence for dementia versus depressive pseudodementia as 'lacking'. In group comparison, psychiatric patients show no significant hypometabolism versus controls; the dorsal anterior cingulate is the discriminating region for bvFTD.

entities.name: Idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus
entities.summary: Dorsal striatal (caudate and putamen) hypometabolism with preserved cortical CONVEXITY metabolism, plus periventricular hypometabolism in caudate, thalamus and cingulate, with relative paracentral / vertex HYPERmetabolism.
entities.discriminator: The midbrain is not part of the iNPH pattern, so midbrain hypometabolism should send you back to PSP — the classic confusion, and the one that leads to futile shunting. Note this is an INFERENCE: neither source paper measured midbrain metabolism in iNPH versus PSP.
entities.mainMimic: PSP shares magnetic gait, falls, frontal slowing and urinary urgency.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Definite iNPH versus controls sens 100% / spec 96%; 96% accuracy versus AD, 100% versus PD. But the pattern has never been tested head-to-head against PSP, MSA or CBD — its comparators were AD and PD only.

patterns.label: iNPH-related pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: Persists after partial-volume correction, so it is not ventricular spill-over.
patterns.caveat: The paracentral hypermetabolism is a covariance-pattern WEIGHT, not measured hypermetabolism. The accuracy figures rest on 11 definite iNPH patients with the threshold optimised in-sample and no external validation, and the pattern has never been tested against PSP, MSA or CBD — its comparators were AD and PD only. AD co-pathology in about 30% of shunted iNPH predicts poorer shunt response, but a positive amyloid PET does not exclude a shunt-responsive component — report both.

entities.name: Autoimmune and paraneoplastic encephalitis
entities.summary: Anti-LGI1 gives medial temporal AND basal ganglia HYPERmetabolism with frontal and parieto-temporal hypometabolism. Anti-NMDAR gives frontotemporal hypermetabolism with occipital hypometabolism.
entities.discriminator: No neurodegenerative disease produces true focal striatal hypermetabolism. Basal ganglia hypermetabolism in an older adult with amnesia and brief dystonic jerks is LGI1 until proven otherwise.
entities.mainMimic: Limbic-predominant degeneration, temporal lobe epilepsy — separated by tempo (weeks to months) and reversibility with immunotherapy.
entities.publishedAccuracy: Anti-LGI1: 13/13 PET scans abnormal versus 6/14 MRI (43%). But in an unselected autoimmune-encephalitis cohort FDG was abnormal in 52/61 (85%) versus MRI 23/57 (40%), and MOST abnormalities were HYPOmetabolism — only 3% had isolated hypermetabolism.

patterns.label: Anti-LGI1
patterns.evidenceNote: Sadaghiani 2023, n=13 — every PET abnormal.
patterns.caveat: Scan BEFORE steroids — steroids abolish the hypermetabolic signature. The hot territory is wider than the classic teaching: medial temporal cortex and nuclei, basal ganglia, AND brainstem and cerebellum.

patterns.label: Anti-NMDAR — anterior–posterior gradient
patterns.evidenceNote: Severity-graded and reversible; described by Leypoldt and Probasco.
patterns.caveat: Anti-NMDAR is precisely the antibody that does NOT behave like a limbic encephalitis — the hot temporal cortex here is lateral and polar, not entorhinal, so the medial temporal cortex is left unshaded. The gradient runs frontal-hot to occipital-cold through an intermediate posterior midline. The teaching that autoimmune limbic encephalitis equals medial temporal hypermetabolism is wrong in most patients.

patterns.label: The commoner reality — hypometabolism (regions illustrative)
patterns.evidenceNote: Probasco 2017: in an unselected cohort most abnormalities were hypometabolism; only 3% had isolated hypermetabolism.
patterns.caveat: Do not exclude autoimmune encephalitis because the scan is not 'hot'.

entities.name: Prion disease — sporadic CJD, Heidenhain variant, fatal familial insomnia
entities.summary: Patchy asymmetric cortical with striatal and thalamic hypometabolism, typically less extensive than the DWI abnormality. Fatal familial insomnia gives severe symmetric thalamic hypometabolism.
entities.discriminator: The hippocampus does NOT show significant metabolic change in prion disease — a useful negative sign against AD and LATE. In FFI the thalamic defect is essentially universal and often present while MRI is still normal.
entities.mainMimic: Heidenhain occipital pattern is confusable with PCA, DLB and an eyes-closed acquisition artefact — tempo settles it.
entities.publishedAccuracy: FDG is not in any prion diagnostic criteria; its role is to raise suspicion, not to confirm. CSF RT-QuIC sens 0.91, spec 0.97 — but sensitivity is LOW in FFI and GSS.

patterns.label: Sporadic CJD
patterns.evidenceNote: Descriptive; patchy and asymmetric by nature.
patterns.asymmetry: Characteristically asymmetric — and the side and the parcels shown are ARBITRARY. This is one instance of a patchy distribution, not a reproducible signature.
patterns.caveat: Read the shaded parcels as an EXAMPLE, not a signature: the location varies case to case, and the FDG deficit is typically less extensive than the DWI abnormality. The hippocampal sparing is the one genuinely published negative here, and it argues against AD and LATE. DWI MRI — cortical ribboning plus caudate and putamen restriction — is the imaging gold standard, not FDG.

patterns.label: Heidenhain variant
patterns.evidenceNote: Marked occipital hypometabolism with corresponding occipital DWI restriction.
patterns.caveat: Tempo — weeks, not years — is what separates this from PCA.

patterns.label: Fatal familial insomnia
patterns.evidenceNote: Cortelli 1997 — severe symmetric thalamic hypometabolism, essentially universal and often the earliest abnormality.
patterns.caveat: Bilateral thalamic hypometabolism in a rapidly progressive dementia should prompt PRNP sequencing and a polysomnogram, not just a CJD panel. RT-QuIC is frequently negative in FFI.

entities.name: Seizure-related — TLE and transient epileptic amnesia
entities.summary: Interictal regional hypometabolism characteristically LARGER than the epileptogenic zone — lateral temporal, temporal pole, ipsilateral thalamus and frontal operculum. Ictal scans show focal hypermetabolism with propagation.
entities.discriminator: The lateral spread beyond the hippocampus is what distinguishes this from a limbic-predominant degeneration.
entities.mainMimic: LATE/LANS, hippocampal sclerosis of ageing, autoimmune limbic encephalitis.
entities.publishedAccuracy: No study has measured how well interictal temporal hypometabolism is separated from limbic-predominant degeneration. The often-quoted sens 95.3% / spec 8.8% (Guo 2021) is a surgical-outcome statistic for PET/MRI in 98 operated patients and does not address that question.

patterns.label: Interictal TLE
patterns.evidenceNote: The classic interictal finding.
patterns.asymmetry: Unilateral, ipsilateral to the seizure focus. The side shown is ARBITRARY.
patterns.caveat: The teaching point is WIDTH, not depth — the deficit spreads laterally well beyond the hippocampus, which is what separates it from a limbic-predominant degeneration. The guideline requires that FDG not be injected in an ictal or postictal state.

patterns.label: Ictal
patterns.evidenceNote: Focal hypermetabolism with propagation-network involvement and contralateral cerebellar hypermetabolism.
patterns.asymmetry: Unilateral; the side shown is ARBITRARY. Cerebellar involvement is CONTRALATERAL to the focus.
patterns.caveat: An ictal injection is a protocol failure, not a diagnostic option — the guideline requires that FDG not be given in an ictal or postictal state.

patterns.label: Postictal
patterns.evidenceNote: Mixed hypo- and hypermetabolism with crossed cerebellar diaschisis; the disturbance can persist for days.
patterns.asymmetry: Unilateral; the side shown is ARBITRARY. The cerebellar effect is CONTRALATERAL and, unlike the ictal state, is HYPOmetabolic.
patterns.caveat: Crossed cerebellar DIASCHISIS is the postictal finding and it is COLD — the opposite of the ictal cerebellar hypermetabolism on the plate before it. Mistaking one for the other is the commonest postictal misread.

entities.name: Wernicke encephalopathy, Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol-related brain damage
entities.summary: Chronic Korsakoff: thalamus and mammillary bodies bilaterally, the entire cingulate cortex, superior and middle frontal cortex, supplementary motor area, precuneus and cuneus.
entities.discriminator: The middle cingulate cortex was the only region with BOTH grey-matter loss and hypometabolism in all 9 patients of the reference series.
entities.mainMimic: Medial thalamic hypometabolism with amnesia is also fatal familial insomnia, anti-Ma2 encephalitis, artery of Percheron infarct, deep cerebral venous thrombosis, Wilson disease and top-of-the-basilar stroke.
entities.publishedAccuracy: No accuracy figures. The Wernicke triad is complete in fewer than 20% — use Caine criteria. No ACUTE Wernicke plate is drawn: the reported mammillary, medial thalamic and periaqueductal hypermetabolism is anecdotal and should not be used as a branch point.

patterns.label: Chronic Korsakoff syndrome
patterns.evidenceNote: Pitel 2009, n=9.
patterns.caveat: The mammillary bodies are NOT drawn. FreeSurfer's ventral diencephalon label would be the nearest parcel, but it is dominated by hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra and red nucleus — shading it would assert nigral and subthalamic hypometabolism that no source supports, in a deck that also teaches PSP and Wilson disease. The mammillary body is in any case an MRI checkpoint (T2/FLAIR/DWI signal, enhancement, atrophy), not an FDG one, and at PET resolution a 4 mm structure is dominated by partial volume. The middle cingulate is the stated discriminator, but the precuneus and superior frontal gyrus were equally consistent metabolically across all 9 patients.

patterns.label: Alcohol-related brain damage
patterns.evidenceNote: Diffuse frontal and superior VERMIAN hypometabolism, partly reversible with abstinence.
patterns.caveat: The cerebellar finding is SUPERIOR VERMIAN. FreeSurfer's cerebellar cortex label cannot isolate the vermis, so the whole label is shaded at a deliberately low grade — do not read this as the pancerebellar loss of MSA, Niemann-Pick C or a spinocerebellar ataxia. Partly reversible with abstinence — repeat rather than commit.

entities.name: Traumatic encephalopathy syndrome / CTE
entities.summary: There is NO validated FDG PET pattern for CTE. Reports of frontotemporal, anterior temporal, thalamic or cerebellar hypometabolism come from small uncontrolled series.
entities.discriminator: None. CTE remains a neuropathological diagnosis and cannot be made in life.
entities.mainMimic: Depression, PTSD, sleep apnoea, chronic pain and opioid use, substance use, the sequelae of a single moderate-severe TBI — and ordinary AD, FTD, ALS or DLB in someone who happened to play contact sports.
entities.publishedAccuracy: None. Commercial SPECT-based 'CTE diagnosis' claims are not supported. Tau PET is not diagnostic at the individual level: flortaucipir uptake in former NFL players overlapped substantially with controls and showed no association with cognitive or neuropsychiatric test performance — though it DID correlate with years of football played (r = 0.45–0.58).

patterns.label: No validated FDG pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: Deliberately left UNSHADED. Every other plate in this atlas is coloured; this one is not, because the correct teaching is the absence itself. Drawing the claimed regions in the same visual grammar as PSP or DLB would hand the reader a picture to remember long after the disclaimer is forgotten — and the claims come from the very uncontrolled series the plate exists to discount.
patterns.caveat: Small uncontrolled series have reported frontotemporal, anterior temporal, thalamic and cerebellar hypometabolism; none is replicated or controlled, and the reported distribution is in any case indistinguishable from depression, PTSD and alcohol-related change — the very differentials that matter here. TES is not CTE: applied to retired contact-sport athletes the criteria show high sensitivity but poor specificity, and a large fraction of unaffected athletes meet them. CTE remains a neuropathological diagnosis. Use standard AD/FTD biomarkers first.

entities.name: Treatable and metabolic 'don't miss' entities
entities.summary: Wilson disease reduces lentiform metabolism, described even in neurologically presymptomatic patients, with cerebellar and variable cortical reduction. NBIA/PKAN gives striatal and pallidal hypometabolism. Niemann-Pick type C gives cerebellar and cortical hypometabolism with a vertical supranuclear saccade palsy that mimics PSP.
entities.discriminator: Age. A movement disorder with striatal hypometabolism in someone under 50 demands a metabolic and genetic workup before any degenerative label.
entities.mainMimic: These mimic PSP, HD and CBS — and unlike them, several are treatable.
entities.publishedAccuracy: No FDG accuracy figures; MRI and genetics carry the diagnosis in all of these. Only the Wilson pattern has any primary FDG citation, and that could not be retrieved for this deck — the NBIA and Niemann-Pick maps have no primary FDG reference at all and are illustrative.

patterns.label: Wilson disease
patterns.evidenceNote: Hawkins 1987; partly reversible with decoppering.
patterns.caveat: The midbrain is deliberately NOT shaded: the midbrain sign in Wilson disease is the MRI 'face of the giant panda', not FDG hypometabolism, and shading it would make this look like the PSP plate. 'Variable cortical reduction' is drawn as a light diffuse wash rather than a frontal predominance, which the source does not support. Kayser-Fleischer rings are present in essentially all neurological Wilson disease; caeruloplasmin <0.1 g/L, 24-hour urinary copper >40 µg, Leipzig score ≥4, ATP7B sequencing.

patterns.label: NBIA / PKAN — no established pattern
patterns.evidenceNote: Descriptive only, and with no primary FDG reference: the regions shown are illustrative. MRI and genetics carry this diagnosis.
patterns.caveat: The 'eye of the tiger' sign is present in >99% of molecularly confirmed classic PKAN but may be absent early and is mimicked by MPAN.

patterns.label: Niemann-Pick type C
patterns.evidenceNote: Descriptive; a recognised PSP mimic through the vertical saccade palsy.
patterns.caveat: Midbrain shading is mechanistically motivated — the vertical saccade palsy localises to the rostral interstitial nucleus of the MLF — but it is not a measured FDG finding, and it is what makes this a PSP mimic. Vertical supranuclear SACCADE palsy in a young patient with splenomegaly is the treatable PSP mimic.
